deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page): a curve f(x,y) = y^m + f_1(x) y^{m-1} + ... + f_m(x) = 0, with the f_i polynomials. (ξ,η) is a point on the curve. ξ is not an x-value where f = 0 and ∂f/∂y = 0 hold for the same y, so (ξ,η) is not a branch point. Riemann asserts that a rational function φ(x,y,ξ,η) exists satisfying three conditions.

(1) Finite points other than ξ (previous page). At every finite x0 ≠ ξ, each Puiseux expansion of φ in x−x0 starts with an exponent > −1.

(2) Points over ξ (completed on this page). On the branch where y=η at x=ξ, the leading term is (x−ξ)^{-1}. On the other m−1 branches over x=ξ, the leading exponent is > −1.

(3) Infinity. Every expansion in falling powers of x, valid for large x, has the form (1/m) x^{-1} + lower terms.

Modern reading (my gloss). Take a place with ramification index e, local parameter t, x − x0 = t^e, dx = e t^{e−1} dt. If φ ~ (x−x0)^α with α > −1, then eα is an integer > −e, so eα ≥ 1−e. Hence φ dx = O(t^{eα+e−1}) dt is holomorphic. So:
- (1) says φ dx is holomorphic at all finite places except those over ξ.
- (2) says φ dx has a simple pole with residue +1 at (ξ,η) and is regular at the other points over ξ.
- (3): at a place over ∞ with x = t^{-e}, dx = −e t^{-e−1} dt, so φ dx ≈ −(e/m) dt/t. That is a simple pole of residue −e/m. Since Σe = m, the residues at infinity total −1, which matches the +1 at (ξ,η) (residue theorem).

Thus φ dx is an abelian differential of the third kind. It has logarithmic poles at (ξ,η) (residue 1) and at ∞, with the residue −1 spread uniformly (−e/m per place) over the places at infinity. It is determined only up to adding first-kind differentials.

Second construction. Let G(x,y) be a polynomial (the word 'ganze' is struck or underlined), chosen 'in the most general way' so that:
- G/f', with f' = ∂f/∂y, has all leading exponents > −1 at every finite x0;
- at infinity, all leading exponents are < −1.

By the same local computation (at ∞: exponent α < −1 gives −eα ≥ e+1, so φ dx = O(t^0) dt), G dx/f_y is holomorphic everywhere, i.e. an abelian differential of the first kind. Riemann states that G then contains p (written ρ on the next page) arbitrary coefficients. The next page continues: G/f' = C_1 φ_1 + ... + C_p φ_p, i.e. a basis of the p-dimensional space of holomorphic differentials, p = genus.

Purpose: this is the setup for the normal integrals ω_α = ∫φ_α dx and Ω = ∫φ(x,y,ξ,η) dx. The next page then gives the exchange (interchange of argument and parameter) relation for ∂φ/∂ξ − ∂/∂x φ(ξ,η,x,y).
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

Unstated assumption: a φ meeting conditions (1)-(3) exists but is not unique. One can add any Σ C_α φ_α, since conditions (1)-(3) are unchanged by adding holomorphic differentials. 'lässt sich bestimmen' asserts existence only; the normalization comes later.
Unstated assumption: condition (3) as written (each infinite expansion begins (1/m)x^{-1}) quietly uses that the residues at infinity sum to −1. This is consistent, since Σe = m, but is not proved.
Unproved claim: the statement that G has exactly p arbitrary coefficients is the dimension theorem for holomorphic differentials, asserted without proof here. Riemann proves it elsewhere (1857).

results.what: Algebraic characterization of a normalized abelian differential of the third kind φ dx. It is given by local Puiseux-expansion conditions: simple pole of residue 1 at (ξ,η), residue −1/m spread over the m sheets at infinity, regular elsewhere.
results.modern_name: Abelian differential (integral) of the third kind / elementary normal integral; meromorphic differential with prescribed simple poles and residues
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, 1857). The algebraic-expansion formulation with normalization at infinity resembles Weierstrass's lectures (1860s–1875) and later Kronecker/Hensel–Landsberg.

results.what: First-kind differentials written as G(x,y) dx / f_y(x,y), with G polynomial constrained by local expansion conditions at finite points and infinity; the space has dimension p.
results.modern_name: Holomorphic differentials as adjoint forms G dx/f_y; dim H^0(K) = genus
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1857 (dimension p); adjoint-polynomial formulation by Riemann, Clebsch–Gordan (1866), Brill–Noether (1874).

results.what: Criterion that a leading Puiseux exponent > −1 at finite points (< −1 at infinity) is equivalent to holomorphy of the differential, including at branch points.
results.modern_name: Order of a differential in a local uniformizing parameter

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard foundation of Riemann's theory of abelian integrals: normal integrals of the first and third kind, with the space of first-kind differentials of dimension p. It is phrased algebraically via expansions, as in his 1857 paper and lectures. The specific normalization (residue −1/m per sheet at infinity) is a minor presentational detail similar to Weierstrass's later treatment. Nothing new relative to what is known as Riemann's.

checkable.sympy: x,xi=symbols('x xi'); eta=sqrt(xi**3-xi); y=sqrt(x**3-x); phi=(y+eta)/(2*y*(x-xi)); limit(((x-xi)*phi).subs(xi,2),x,2)
checkable.asserts: Example on the elliptic curve y^2=x^3-x (m=2), with my candidate φ=(y+η)/(2y(x−ξ)). On the sheet y=η the residue at x=ξ=2 is 1 (limit equals 1).
On the other sheet y=−η over ξ=2, φ is regular: the limit is 0 (numerator vanishes), so the leading exponent is > −1, matching condition (2).
Condition (3): at infinity φ ~ (1/m) x^{-1} with m=2, so the limit equals 1/2.
For y^2=x^5−x, G=x has G/f' ~ x^{-3/2}/2, degree < −1 at infinity (x·G/f' → 0). G=1 and G=x both qualify, G=x^2 does not, so p=2.
G=x^2 fails the infinity condition (the limit is infinite: degree −1/2 is not < −1), so the hyperelliptic genus-2 curve has exactly p=2 first-kind differentials.
